title: Night prayer
hook: the short prayer before sleep, with the Nunc Dimittis of Simeon
carry: now let your servant go in peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Office, the Church's clock of psalms: someone is always praying. Today, the last hour of that clock.

The lights go down in a monastery chapel. The day's work is over, the last guests have gone, and the monks file in for one more short hour of prayer before bed. It's gentle, almost a lullaby: a look back over the day, a psalm about resting under God's wings, a few lines of reading. And it ends with a man in the Temple, holding a baby, saying he can go in peace. Then the lights go out, and nobody speaks until morning. Today's word is that last hour.
screen: `LIGHTS DOWN IN THE CHAPEL.` → `A SHORT, GENTLE HOUR.` → `A MAN HOLDING A BABY.`

segments.voice: Compline comes from the Latin completorium, the completing: the hour that finishes the day. First, the shape. It begins by looking back. In today's Liturgy of the Hours there's a short examination of conscience: what did today hold, what do I regret, what am I grateful for. Then a psalm or two; on Sundays, Psalm 90 in the Douay numbering, the psalm about resting in the shadow of the Most High. Then a short reading, and a response taken from the psalms: into thy hands I commend my spirit. In Luke, Jesus says that line on the cross. Said at bedtime, the echo is hard to miss. Second, the song at its heart: the canticle of Simeon, from Luke's Gospel. Mary and Joseph bring the infant Jesus to the Temple. A just and devout man named Simeon had been promised he wouldn't die before he saw the Christ. He takes the baby in his arms and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation." In Latin it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss, and that's its name. Third, why at night. Simeon is ready to let go. He's seen what he waited for, and he can rest. The Church sets his words at the edge of sleep, a small daily practice of letting go. Fourth, the close: a hymn to Mary, often the Salve Regina, and then the house keeps silence until morning.
screen: `COMPLETORIUM: THE COMPLETING.` · `LOOK BACK, A PSALM, INTO THY HANDS.` · `SIMEON HOLDS THE CHILD.` · `A DAILY PRACTICE OF LETTING GO.` · then, large: `NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT, O LORD.`

segments.voice: Look back over today, quickly and kindly: one thing you regret, one thing you're grateful for. Then, if you pray, say Simeon's words slowly: Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace. If you don't pray, picture Simeon handing the baby back, and let your own day be handed back too.
Compline. From the Latin for completing: the last hour of the Church's day, prayed before sleep, with the song of Simeon at its heart. Today's word.
Your line: now let your servant go in peace. A finished day can be let go. Day two hundred forty-one, and good night.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns pray Compline together before the night silence, and other Catholics pray it alone from a breviary or an app; it includes an examination of conscience, psalms, a short reading, the Nunc Dimittis and a closing antiphon to Mary.

original.note: Latin: now you dismiss. the first words of Simeon's song in the Latin Bible, and its name.

chat.says: Why does night prayer end with that old man holding a baby?
options: It's Simeon's song: he's seen what he waited for and can let go in peace.
It's Simeon's song, sung at night because he met the baby late in the evening.
It's a lullaby to remember the night Jesus was born in Bethlehem.
